speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This framework for dual listings puts in place the option for SGX to enhance its connectivity with other markets.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It also streamlines our regulatory requirements for dual listings.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Other initiatives announced by the Equities Market Review Group last year to support the demand and supply of capital include the Equity Market Development Programme, which will allocate up to $6.5 billion directly and also to crowd in private capital to deepen local fund management capabilities and enhance trading liquidity, as well as measures to strengthen equities research coverage.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Following the announcement of these measures, the Singapore market has seen some positive momentum.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Moving forward now with the GLB will help us to capitalise on this momentum to further raise Singapore's standing as a listing venue of choice, where issuers with good potential can access funding to grow into regional and global champions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Currently, issuers who wish to concurrently list on SGX and another overseas exchange may face differing requirements across jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is a duplication of effort to meet two sets of requirements, even in the case where the general regulatory principles that underpin the listing process are broadly similar across the jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In this context, "same-same but different" is not as ideal as "exactly same-same" because the former still increases compliance costs.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The proposed legislative framework addresses this concern by harmonising and streamlining requirements for concurrent dual listings on SGX and an eligible overseas exchange.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The approach reduces regulatory compliance costs while upholding high standards.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dual listings can bring benefits for many stakeholders in Singapore's equities market ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the case of the GLB, regional issuers will have easier access to complementary sets of investors on both exchanges, while benefiting from better brand recognition.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through this, the GLB can attract more diverse issuers to list in Singapore, which will add energy and dynamism to our equities market.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This in turn creates opportunities for local service providers, including lawyers, accountants and other financial intermediaries.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Investors will also gain access to a broader range of high-quality investment opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Bill will position Singapore to capture future opportunities, where dual listings from other reputable jurisdictions, with comparable disclosure requirements and which adhere to international standards, can be facilitated.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There has been broad industry support for this Bill and the GLB.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MAS has considered the feedback received and taken them on board where appropriate.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A new section Part 13A, which sets up a framework to support dual listing arrangements between SGX and an appropriate overseas exchange, such as in the case of the GLB.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Other amendments to the SFA, which will support all listings, including listings on the GLB.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These amendments are needed to facilitate the harmonisation of key aspects of the fundraising and listing process for dual listings, and to reduce the friction and compliance burden faced by issuers while maintaining robust standards.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This provides a framework to support dual listing arrangements, such as the GLB.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, it sets out the key criteria that such partnerships for dual listing arrangements must satisfy.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, it empowers MAS to set regulations to close differences in the securities laws of Singapore and a foreign jurisdiction to facilitate the dual listing partnership, subject to safeguards and maintaining robust regulatory standards.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The new Part 13A defines the nature of any dual listing arrangement between Singapore and another jurisdiction that can be supported by new MAS regulations.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MAS will exercise the powers under the new Part 13A only if the following considerations are met.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, the dual listing arrangement in consideration enhances issuers' access to a larger pool of liquidity and a broader range of investors.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, the overseas exchange is from a jurisdiction with securities laws consistent with the International Organisation of Securities Commissions' (IOSCO) international standards and principles, particularly regarding enforcement, regulatory cooperation and disclosure requirements.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the case of the GLB, Nasdaq and the United States (US) meet these conditions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Nasdaq is one of the largest stock exchanges globally, providing access to deep pools of capital.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The US, like Singapore, adopts IOSCO's international standards and principles for financial markets regulation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These qualifying criteria also apply to future arrangements with compatible jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Part 13A empowers MAS to make regulations to vary the application of specific market misconduct and offer-related provisions in Part 12 and 13 of the SFA.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It enables MAS to formulate and make adjustments to regulatory requirements in a timely manner.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Based on engagements with market practitioners and prospective issuers, three main areas have been identified where modifications will be made to the existing SFA regulatory regime for dual listing arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These areas are intended to facilitate a smooth dual listing process and post-listing operations.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Currently, issuers seeking concurrent listings must prepare two sets of prospectuses based on two sets of disclosure requirements, one for each jurisdiction, resulting in additional complexity and costs.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Bill addresses this, by enabling MAS to set regulations to modify offer-related provisions to facilitate the use of a single set of offer documents.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MAS and SGX will review the prospectus and listing application under these aligned requirements.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This minimises friction when preparing the offer documents while maintaining information value for investors, since both the US and Singapore's disclosure requirements are aligned with international standards.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Issuers seeking a concurrent listing may encounter significant friction from different filing requirements and timelines.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Under Part 13A, MAS can make regulations to address procedural and timing differences between two jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Differences in permitted market practices can create friction and uncertainty for dual-listed issuers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For the GLB, there are certain standard US market practices, such as the issuance of forward-looking statements, which are permitted by well-established US safe harbours.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Bill will enable MAS to set regulations to adopt safe harbours as defences to the market misconduct provisions in the SFA.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They do not provide a valid defence against criminal liability for fraud or dishonest conduct.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MAS and the relevant Singapore authorities will retain full discretion to enforce against any misconduct that occurs in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our regulatory oversight and enforcement responsibilities remain unchanged.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If there is a cross-border misconduct, MAS and the relevant Singapore authorities will work with foreign regulators and law enforcement counterparts to coordinate our investigation and enforcement actions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singapore investors will also continue to be able to seek recourse for losses arising from such breaches under the investor recourse provisions in the SFA.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This Bill also contains other amendments to the SFA which will facilitate the offering process for all listings in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, issuers will be allowed to engage retail investors based on preliminary prospectuses rather than only using the final prospectuses.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Industry feedback shows that this will be useful to enable a better gauge of market demand and for investors to have more time to familiarise themselves with an initial public offering (IPO).

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This change will apply to all IPOs, including those on the GLB.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To protect investors, such engagements will be subject to safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, no offers can be made on the basis of the preliminary prospectus, and the document must also state clearly that its content is subject to further changes.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, we have received feedback that the regulatory treatment for Depositary Receipt (DR) offerings involving new underlying shares requires greater clarity.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With DRs, companies raise funds by issuing shares that are deposited with a financial institution or depositary.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The depositary issues DRs representing the underlying shares, which are then offered and sold to investors.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is to ensure that investors receive information directly from the company whose shares they are investing in.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will facilitate the disclosure of relevant information for all DR offerings on SGX, including those on the GLB.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The dual listings framework and the GLB are parts of a broader strategic move to reinforce Singapore's position as a leading financial centre and a vibrant hub for capital market activities.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are creating new pathways for issuers to access deeper pools of international capital while broadening investors' access to new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will lay the groundwork for greater market depth and maturity, and open the door for future partnerships and possibilities for SGX, issuers and investors alike.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have been in the Chamber for about five hours, so, I propose to take a break now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.59 pm until 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is part of the suite of recommendations by the Equities Market Review Group, chaired by Minister Chee Hong Tat, in its final report issued in November 2025.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The recommendations are a timely intervention to revitalise our equities market by capitalising on our strengths in connectivity and a high starting base of robust regulation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This can allow us to capture smaller- and mid-sized enterprises which are not well served by the US markets alone, as those markets are driven by mega-cap firms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just as a sample size, may I ask the Minister how many Asian companies had a market capitalisation of at least $2 billion in each of the last 10 years?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By way of illustration, what are some examples of the "smaller- and mid-sized enterprises" that we are looking to attract?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Being a novel mechanism, attracting notable companies to list as "poster child" listings could have a significant effect in encouraging issuer and investor interest.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If there has not been firm commitments or interest by companies to come onboard, what specific publicity avenues are being planned so that we can attract issuers to utilise this new mechanism?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would there be further incentives to stimulate issuer interest?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More broadly, beyond the number of listings, how will MAS assess whether dual listings will translate into sustained liquidity and meaningful price discovery in Singapore, rather than trading activity gravitating primarily to the larger overseas market?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hear Minister Chee's opening remarks just now and he has alluded to the ancillary services benefiting and others, but this is a more specific question in terms of price discovery and sustained liquidity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, the new Part 13A has also been drawn up in a non-exhaustive manner, as MAS may prescribe other tie-ups with overseas exchanges as Dual Listing Boards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister clarify if the SGX-Nasdaq tie-up is intended as a pilot exercise, whose outcomes will be assessed before further dual listing arrangements are pursued?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Or are we already in advanced discussions with other exchanges to broaden this network?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next question is whether the proposed legislative provisions is sufficiently flexible to facilitate listings across three or more exchanges in future, for example, a triple listing involving SGX, Nasdaq and an European exchange, or would further legislative amendments be required?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we expand such cross-border arrangements, how will MAS guard against regulatory arbitrage, where issuers may structure offerings to benefit from the most lenient aspects of different jurisdictions, and ensure that our standards of disclosure, governance and enforcement are not diluted over time?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there a timeline by which such regulations will be ready, so that the dual listing bridge can be operational?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would commend the explicit power under the new section 309G(2) to incorporate foreign securities laws by reference.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This reduces administrative burden and allows us to leverage established regulatory frameworks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, may I clarify whether foreign precedents and case law would guide the interpretation of these provisions locally, or whether Singapore will retain full autonomy in applying these rules within our own legal context?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is also the issue of compatibility with broader legal frameworks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will we be reviewing such areas as part of strengthening investor protection, in line with the Equities Market Review Group's recommendations?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Related to this, in cases involving cross-border misconduct, where key management, assets or evidence may be located overseas, how will MAS ensure effective enforcement and accountability?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The move to allow earlier engagement with investors, including retail investors, is a notable shift too.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It broadens access and allows more inclusive participation, which is positive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, at early stages, information is still evolving, disclosures are not finalised and retail investors may be more susceptible to sentiment or incomplete narratives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The question I have is: how will MAS ensure that retail investors are not unduly influenced by preliminary or incomplete information?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And will there be enhanced investor education or disclosure safeguards to help retail investors better understand the limitations of such early-stage information?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, Mr Deputy Speaker, it is on Sponsored Depositary Receipts (SDRs).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The clarification on SDRs is a sensible and important step.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That said, I would like to better understand how MAS intends to operationalise this in practice.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will MAS ensure that disclosure standards for SDRs remain fully aligned with those expected of primary listings, so that investors are not exposed to uneven information standards?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Further, given the cross-border nature of such instruments, how will MAS ensure effective enforcement and accountability where the underlying issuer is based overseas?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the Review Group has recognised, there is no "silver bullet", a holistic ecosystem-wide approach is required.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are we seeing measurable outcomes from the earlier initiatives and what review timelines are in place to refine or recalibrate policies?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In other words, a bit more other than what Minister Chee has already alluded to earlier in his opening speech.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin):   This Bill may appear to be merely a set of technical amendments to securities law, but it is, in fact, responding to a very real problem.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Today, when a company decides where to raise capital, it is not simply a question of whether it can list.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is a question of where the money is, where the investors are, where the analysts are and whether the processes are smooth and the rules are clear.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Simply put, competition in capital markets is not just about having the right institutions in place; it is about whether the market is large enough, active enough and accessible enough.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If a company feels that listing on another market would give it greater visibility, more active trading and a fairer valuation, it will naturally choose to go there.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: That is the reality and we cannot avoid it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I therefore believe that the significance of this Bill lies not merely in amending a few laws, but in helping to clear the path and build the bridges for Singapore's capital market, so that capital, companies and investors are more willing to come.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But if these things are not done properly, even the best conditions will attract few takers.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The problem many companies face today is not that they are unwilling to comply with rules, but that they have to do the same thing twice or even three times.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Listing documents have to be prepared in multiple sets; approval processes have to be gone through multiple times.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Anyone who has run a business knows that it is rarely one big problem that slows things down – it is the accumulation of many small, repetitive ones that makes everything feel increasingly burdensome.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Over time, companies are not deterred by strictness; they are deterred by repetition and hassle.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, if we can reduce this unnecessary duplication and make processes smoother, it would be a very practical help to companies and would also attract more of them to list in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: That said, as we simplify processes, we must also preserve Singapore's longstanding strengths: transparency, clarity and trustworthiness.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We cannot just be fast; we must also be steady and precise.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is good for everyone in the long run.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The earlier a company helps the market understand what it does, how it makes money and what its risks are, the easier it is for investors to make informed judgements and the more likely it is that pricing will be fair.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is like buying a flat – if the buyer gets to see the information early, they can form a clearer picture.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If communication happens too early and only the positive aspects are presented, investors may be unduly influenced and by the time the risks become apparent, it may be too late.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The key principle, therefore, is this: earlier engagement is acceptable, but it must not become earlier promotion.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Companies cannot lead with only the good news and leave the important risks to be disclosed later.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I would therefore suggest that the regulatory authorities, in addition to setting legal minimum standards, also provide clearer guidance so that companies, intermediaries and advisers all know what is and is not permissible.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In simple terms, investors sometimes hold not shares directly, but a certificate representing those shares.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The party that best understands the company's business and risks is the company itself.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is like sending a parcel – if the contents were mislabelled to begin with, you cannot simply blame the delivery person; the responsibility lies at the source.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In practice, however, cross-border structures can be very complex.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A company may be incorporated in one country, the intermediary based in another and the investors located elsewhere still.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If something does go wrong, figuring out who investors should approach and how to seek redress may not be straightforward.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I would therefore suggest that as the Government clarifies legal liability, it should also strengthen cross-border regulatory cooperation and enhance investor education, so that people not only understand what the law says but also know what to do when problems arise. : Mr Deputy Speaker, beyond market structure and efficiency, this Bill is also an opportunity to strengthen Singapore's position in sustainable finance.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As more investors globally allocate capital based on environmental, social and governance considerations, our regulatory framework should continue to support high quality, consistent sustainability disclosures.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This will not only protect investors from greenwashing but also give credible companies greater confidence to raise capital here.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Another area worth considering is the role of technology and digitalisation in capital markets.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: With increasing use of digital platforms, algorithmic trading and tokenised securities, regulatory clarity must keep pace with innovation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While we support efficiency and accessibility, safeguards must remain robust to manage new forms of risk, including market volatility and cybersecurity threats.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should also take this opportunity to further strengthen retail investor participation in our market.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Continued efforts in financial literacy, transparency of products and accessibility of information will help build broader and more resilient participation over time.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our reputation has been built over decades, and it remains one of the strongest advantages.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin):   Because this Bill has identified an important key point: if Singapore is to continue as an international financial centre, it cannot rely solely on its past strengths, nor simply on "the stability we have always had." Stability is important, but markets also need vitality.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Openness is important, but responsibilities must be clearly defined.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Efficiency is important, but investor trust matters even more.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As the saying goes, “Water can carry a boat, but it can also capsize it”.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I rise in support of this Bill, and I commend MAS and the Ministry of Finance for moving this Bill with urgency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The GLB represents Singapore's most ambitious structural intervention in its equity markets in a generation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That ambition is necessary, but ambition alone will not deliver outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It must be matched by execution in the realities of our market.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I note that the regulatory appetite for this move reflects a shift.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A decade ago, MAS often maintained a broad scepticism toward special purpose acquisition companies and novel fund structures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, it is more prepared to engage with innovation in a calibrated way.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That shift, while long overdue, is nevertheless welcome.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But this House has a responsibility not only to support ambition, but to test it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I speak today not to oppose the Bill, but to provide constructive views so that it delivers genuine market vibrancy, rather than the appearance of it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The fundamentals of our equity market remain fragile.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In terms of cash equity trading, the Hong Kong market is more than 20 times more liquid than our own.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are the baseline realities against which this Bill must be measured.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I welcome the GLB.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The new Part 13A allows MAS to modify and align regulatory requirements with overseas exchanges to support dual listings and streamline offer documentation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a meaningful step if Singapore is to compete for international listings.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, several structural concerns raised by market practitioners need to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But in practice, only a small number of Southeast Asian companies will meet this bar.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: According to market practitioners, about eight Southeast Asian tech firms would meet the threshold, with another two to three potentially close to achieving that.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a narrow universe when set against the ambitions of the GLB.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The companies large enough to qualify are precisely those that may choose to list directly on Nasdaq, without the need for a Singapore leg.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I ask whether MAS will consider a tiered threshold, or a review mechanism as the market matures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given that Part 13A allows MAS to partner with different overseas exchanges, it would also be helpful to understand which segments of issuers we are prioritising and how Singapore intends to position itself relative to other listing venues competing for the same pool of companies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Institutional investors will trade where liquidity is deepest.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In a dual listing structure, that is likely to be the primary overseas exchange.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If Singapore trading volumes remain thin, issuers will question the purpose of maintaining a listing here.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need clarity on how Singapore intends to support meaningful trading activity on the SGX leg, beyond existing measures, such as retail allocation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Issuers are concerned about the risk of US class action litigation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without clarity on how Singapore-based issuers can navigate these risks, we may deter the very firms we seek to attract.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is particularly relevant in a dual listing framework where issuers are subject to multiple legal regimes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Greater clarity on how these cross-border liabilities are managed will be important for issuer confidence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Under the framework, an issuer delisted from the overseas exchange must also be delisted from the Dual Listing Board.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This creates a structural dependency on that foreign exchange.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I do not question the good faith of any partner exchange.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But I ask the Minister what safeguards exist for investors holding shares on SGX if such a partnership is disrupted and whether extending the framework to other exchanges provid a sufficient hedge?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I welcome the expansion of retail investor access.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The amendments to section 251 allow the issuers to present preliminary offering materials to any person before a prospectus is registered, subject to safeguards.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This levels the playing field between retail and institutional investors and gives Singaporeans earlier access to investment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Earlier access to information is a meaningful change.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, access alone does not guarantee better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If investors receive a preliminary prospectus without the corresponding ability to evaluate it, they are exposed to increased risk rather than be empowered to act.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The safeguards in the Bill, including disclaimers and restrictions on application forms, are necessary, but they do not address this underlying gap in financial literacy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A preliminary prospectus in the hands of an unprepared investor is not empowerment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I must be candid about what this Bill cannot do.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It seeks to attract more issuers and introduces mechanisms, such as SDR, where the issuer of the underlying securities assumes responsibility for disclosure and liability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But a chronic weakness of the SGX is a demand-side problem.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our retail investor base is smaller and more conservative.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is a long-standing preference for dividends, bonds and property over equities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without liquidity, even strong listings may struggle to gain traction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need a whole-of-life-cycle approach to capital markets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Across asset classes including credit, infrastructure and real estate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: MAS has begun moving toward this ecosystem model.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Minister to accelerate this effort and to ensure it is implemented in a coordinated way.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I offer three specific suggestions to strengthen the implementation of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Current consultation materials do not prescribe how settlement, closing and price stabilisation will operate across Nasdaq and SGX.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Early research coverage is essential to building investor confidence, especially for companies unfamiliar to Singapore investors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, the pipeline below the GLB threshold must be developed more deliberately.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I assume the Ministry already has a set of internal key performance indicators (KPIs) for this initiative.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If so, I would encourage that these KPIs be made clear, measurable and where possible, transparent to this House, so that we can assess whether this Bill is delivering its intended outcomes over time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are introducing these reforms at a moment of global market uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Geopolitical tensions and tariff risks are already affecting IPO pipelines.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If the GLB is launched into weak market conditions, we risk building a well-designed framework with limited participation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A framework without issuers is not a market.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the MAS to consider contingency measures, including bridging capital through platforms, such as ADDX and other flexible funding solutions, so that near-IPO companies are not lost due to timing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, ambition alone will not deliver outcomes unless it is matched by execution in the realities of our market.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This debate has made clear what that execution requires.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the GLB, we must ensure that design choices do not constrain the pipeline or weaken Singapore's position in global capital markets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On retail participation, we must ensure that earlier access is matched by investor capability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On market structure, we must address the demand side constraints that continue to limit liquidity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On implementation, we must resolve operational uncertainties and build a credible pipeline under realistic market conditions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They go to the heart of why this Bill matters.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's position as a leading financial hub has never been accidental.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It has been built through deliberate policy choices, strong institutions and our ability to connect global capital with regional opportunity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our financial sector is not peripheral to our economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a core driver of growth, a source of high value jobs and a gateway through which international capital flows into Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we do not continue to strengthen our markets, capital will not stand still.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It will move to where liquidity is deeper, where ecosystems are stronger and where execution is clearer.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, this is not only about introducing a new framework.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about whether Singapore remains a place where global capital chooses to come, where regional companies choose to list and where Singaporeans themselves choose to participate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we match ambition with execution and follow through with discipline in addressing these gaps, then this Bill can do more than improve our market structure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It can reinforce Singapore's role as a trusted financial centre, a gateway to Asia and a platform for long-term growth.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But at the end of the day, we should also be clear about how success will be measured in practical terms.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How much incremental daily trading volume are we seeking to generate?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because that will be one of the clearest indicators of whether these reforms are making a meaningful difference to market activity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that access leads to understanding.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that participation leads to liquidity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And we must ensure that ambition leads to outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And on that basis, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The GLB and the link-up with Nasdaq is a really good move.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: For technology entrepreneurs, the Nasdaq is like a Mecca, dream land, where we go and do listings and if we look at the Magnificent Seven, starting with the letter "A" in the alphabet, which is Amazon; Apple; Google; Tesla; Meta, which was Facebook; Nvidia – they are among the top capitalisation of Nasdaq.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, tying them brings our exchange into a good situation or environment for a very tech-driven future.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The market is dominated by players including the banking services, such as DBS Group, Singtel and ST Engineering.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The capitalisation of the financial services in our stock exchanges is about 40%; 20% for real estates; for IT, 5%.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Or do we also want to build ourselves as the next Nasdaq, where we can actually have more tech and innovation-driven companies on our exchanges?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And if we are looking into the future, with our Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) investments, and all the investment in technology and R&D, I believe that we can actually try to move into that direction.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: There are a couple of questions that I would like to ask.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Based on what we have right now, it is not really big enough for us to have a lot of companies that are "unicorns", grown generically from Singapore, we might have to attract a lot more from the region, or as far as China, or perhaps US.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: What are the competitive advantages and benefits to attract such deep-tech companies overseas to list or to join the GLB?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Will we be encouraging special purpose acquisition companies for GLB?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: For example, in my trade, in the electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) or flying car areas, there are two companies: one is Joby Aviation, and one is Archer Aviation.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: They listed in 2021, on either NYSE or Nasdaq, as special purpose acquisition companies, before they have a certified product.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: When they are listed, they were about $6 billion.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: At the end of the hype, they were down to $2 billion, probably $3 billion.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: But now, with the products being on the way to certification, they are probably worth about $12 billion.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Do we have the policy to stomach that, losing but very high valuation, because of very high potential, and highly scalable?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, when it comes to all these highly scalable companies or tech ventures, would you consider a special pathway for such pre-commercialisation, deep-tech companies, especially in pharma and biotech.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And biotech is one of our key R&D areas in our RIE 2030 plan.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: One of the things I am really concerned with is that, for this $2 billion, how can we help our company, our deep-tech ventures here, slowly move up to being "unicorns".

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, those are the possible options that we can explore for companies based here or developed from our RIE 2030.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am sympathetic to the objectives of the Bill, and for this reason, I see little justification in not supporting it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I will offer some serious points of caution and reprise the broad case that my Sengkang colleague, Mr Louis Chua, and I offered in our joint Adjournment Motion delivered in this House some three months ago, on making Singapore Equities great again.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will also state at the outset that I am the chief economist emeritus of a wealth management and advisory firm, and own a very small number of shares on the SGX.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As context is perhaps helpful to look at how our local stock market has performed of late.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For decades, our local exchange had, in the minds of many observers, underperformed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Listings were woeful and delistings generally far exceeded new listings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With the Main Board dominated by financials and real estate, liquidity has been weak, especially compared to other developed markets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This translated into the benchmark Straits Times Index (STI) going sideways for the better part of the past decade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Things began to look brighter from the middle of 2024, as rising geopolitical tensions and the shift to a more multi-polar world appear to have triggered a structural shift in international financial flows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The STI was reinvigorated and hit new highs and even outperformed global benchmarks like the S&P 500.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It could be a safe harbour for global capital, in the otherwise troubled world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The trick then is to sustain this momentum with concrete policy action that truly shore up liquidity and keep it here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The STI was re-invigorated and hit new highs and even outperformed global benchmarks like the S&P 500.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It could be a safe harbour for global capital, in the otherwise troubled world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The trick then is to sustain this momentum with concrete policy action that truly shore up liquidity and keep it here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The amendments proposed in this Bill seek to do so, but I fear that they do not go far enough.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For me, there is little to quibble with in terms of the language in the new part 13(A).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, I will focus on whether the ostensible goal of dual listing, to stimulate greater liquidity, especially in our local boards, may actually be accomplished.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The evidence suggests caution in arriving at this conclusion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Research does generally support the notion that cross- listings do improve liquidity while boosting valuations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, and this is the key "but", trading and hence the associated liquidity boost tends to concentrate in one dominant exchange.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The one with more liquidity to begin with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Between the SGX and Nasdaq, this will invariably be the latter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our moves to push for dual listing then may paradoxically result in our already scarce local liquidity leaking away into foreign shores.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Recent events lend further credence to this argument.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The stocks trading volume on the SGX has been modest at best.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the listing generated substantial interest, the offering was more than three times over subscribed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Contrast this to volumes of close to two million in its primary US market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even in cases where the SGX collaborated with smaller exchanges, the experience has been disappointing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Secondary listings since 2010 have all been by way of introduction with no new share issuance or capital raising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The dual listing of SP AusNet in Singapore and Australia saw limited interest by SGX investors, despite solid trading volumes on the ASX, before eventually being delisted in 2018.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, increased trading volumes may be accompanied by higher variability in stock market returns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means, especially for our already low liquidity market, that we may also be inviting greater volatility due to this arrangement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Taken together, we must surely be careful for what we wish for when we promote cross listing, especially with a bigger partner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, the motivation for cross listing itself appears rather lukewarm, even in the eyes of the Equity Market Review Group.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The final report does highlight the importance of cross-border partnerships, but it makes only two explicit references to cross-listings in a 39-page 15,000-word report.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of these, only one speaks to a support measure of 180,000 for cross listed Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) in the broader context of the GEMS scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For me, this does not strike one as a ringing endorsement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The natural question then, is how we think this latest foray into cross listing might be different.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What mechanisms are there to this round to ensure that the SGX sustains genuine trading volume rather than being relegated to a secondary venue in all, but name?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What will allow Singapore to become a price-setting market rather than being a pale mirror of the main exchange?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As written, the Bill grants MAS the authority to declare a foreign exchange prescribed, as long as its disclosure standards are comparable to IOSCO's 1998 cross-border disclosure standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This document is nearly 30 years old and the term comparable is discretionary, since MAS' determination faces no defined parliamentary check.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We risk anchoring ourselves to standards that may align on paper, but diverge in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Parliament is effectively being asked to authorise in advance and without details, regulatory changes whose content will only be revealed much later.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I understand that such discretion maybe necessary for operational efficiency, the only investor protection floor given in section 9G(VII) which preserves liability under any law not modified, replaced or disapply, appears somewhat circular.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, the Bill may potentially allow foreign defences to be imported and used against local investors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This effectively leaves us as a standard's taker, rather than standard setter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, the regulatory refinements that allow issuers to disseminate preliminary prospectus is directly to retail investors, outlined in clause 3, and which require the issuer to assume responsibility for registering the prospectus in clause 2, do promote informational exchange.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The ostensible goal here is that by increasing accountability and transparency, liquidity will be further deepened, especially among retail investors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I appreciate the desire to rope in more retail investors and indeed, I had pushed for this in our joint Adjournment Motion by suggesting that Central Provident Fund's (CPF's) impending Life-cycle Retirement Investment Scheme, consider including the local indexes a means of promoting retail ownership, there is nevertheless a risk that preliminary prospectus made available to less sophisticated retail investors may open the door to aggressive marketing and foster excessive hype.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Is there a place for statutory safeguards, especially plain language risk disclosures that highlight differences between American and Singaporean domestic market practices?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More generally, has MAS examined evidence from comparable jurisdictions on the sort of safeguards that have been applied to protect retail participants if indeed they were to receive preliminary material?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As with cross listings, these rules are unobjectionable on their face.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But let us recognise them for what they are, facilitative procedural amendments, rather than deep-seated structural reforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we truly want to improve accountability and transparency, we need to move beyond, and toward ensuring the quality of post listing disclosures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My hon friend, Louis Chua, had previously outlined how such value up assessments will look like – mandatory disclosure of returns on equity or invested capital targets, cost of capital and dividend and stock improvement plans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These remain conspicuously absent thus far in our securities laws.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This Bill offers an ideal opportunity to redress this on a small scale.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For firms seeking a listing on the GLB, we can mandate such disclosures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, these are already large global companies which should well be able to afford the additional cost of such compliance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Doing so, will ensure that such large cap listings actually deliver long-term value to Singaporean shareholders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this Bill is focused on cross-listings with the Nasdaq, one is left to wonder if there are yet more exchanges the MAS is contemplating extending dual listings too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Will Parliament have any role in scrutinising the credibility of these other exchanges before they are designated or liability provisions altered?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As I mentioned in my Adjournment Motion speech two months back, where the capital raising cycle appears to have fallen short is in building market liquidity for raising funds for mid-cap and growth companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Despite the Bill's merits, Singapore's challenge of growing our domestic market in such companies, for me, remains largely unresolved.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Before I begin, I declare that I am the Group Managing Director of Commonwealth Capital Group, a Singapore global enterprise operating a conglomerate of businesses.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: First, global firms with an Asian nexus will benefit from the option of getting the best of both Nasdaq and SGX liquidity pools.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: While Nasdaq offers a deep pool of global capital, investors there may not necessarily have the understanding of the Asian growth story.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: A dual listing on SGX would allow such firms to tap our local liquidity pools, where investors have a better understanding of regional prospects and nuances.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, a more vibrant ecosystem of listings will benefit the financial services industry and create some good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: In short, the financial services sector will not experience jobless growth.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It will also benefit the SGX as one of our local companies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, this could be the first of many other dual listing arrangements, that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim alluded to, which could make the SGX a regional hub for such listings in the future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And perhaps, not just in the technology sector.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: However, like Yip Hon Weng, I believe it is equally important to talk about what dual listing arrangements do not provide on their own.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This is so that we can manage our expectations and can continue to strive towards additional ways to support our equities ecosystem and the growth of our Singapore businesses.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We are unlikely to require overseas firms to have a Singapore presence before listing.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This is understandable; we do not want to increase the barriers for quality growth companies to list here.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: That said, I hope that other Government agencies, like the Economic Development Board, can use this new opportunity to create new jobs for Singaporeans, by encouraging these firms to move some headquarters functions to Singapore after listing.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And for Singaporean firms looking to dual list, I hope that a local listing encourages them to further anchor their headquarters and high value-added functions in Singapore for the long term.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But fundamentally, we must ask ourselves what we want our Singapore stock exchange to accomplish for our broader economy and society – and what it should not accomplish.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We want an avenue for quality Singapore companies to raise growth capital by issuing equity.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Larger, high quality Singapore companies that can achieve a Nasdaq listing already do so and they would continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: They could perhaps be encouraged to dual list in Singapore, with the benefit of some additional liquidity from Asian-focused investors.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But mid-sized companies with a more local or regional presence are unlikely to benefit from this arrangement, as they would not typically be considered for listing on global exchanges like the Nasdaq.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The uncle and auntie in our heartlands should not be seen as the retail investors providing exit liquidity for private capital owners, whether businessmen or fund managers, looking to make a quick buck.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The foundation of a vibrant stock exchange is built on quality companies that attract more investors because these companies are well run, well governed and growing.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We should therefore continually endeavour to raise standards for companies listed on the SGX so that investors continue to come to it to invest in high quality listings.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Some may suggest that we do not have enough quality Singapore companies because we do not have a vibrant SGX.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We do not have a vibrant SGX because we do not yet have enough quality Singapore companies that meet the standard.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: So, we should focus on further improving corporate governance, disclosures and minority investor protections.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Over time, these efforts will make our SGX one that all Singaporeans and Singapore companies can be proud of.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I am heartened to hear Minister Chee's opening speech that trading volume has increased.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But it is still worth asking what impact this Bill will bring to our market and how we bring more private investors in so activity does not just start here, but continues here.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The question we are facing is whether companies will actually come and whether real activity will follow.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I will focus on three areas: (a) the positioning of the GLB; (b) the development of our financial ecosystem; and (c) whether our market is ready.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This is aimed at a narrow group of large, mature and credible companies.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: That is understandable, given how the board is positioned and the quality we want on SGX.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This Bill creates a clearer pathway than before.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But the question is how many companies who meet these criteria are willing and ready to take it up.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The key constraint is whether companies see real value in listing here, given the additional requirements.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Were pre-IPO firms consulted or have any expressed concrete interest in listing under this framework?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The proposed focus on companies with an Asian or regional nexus further narrows the pool.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: While I understand the intent to anchor relevance to our region, having an Asian nexus is one thing, but having a reason to raise capital in Singapore is another.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: While the Bill could help address the long-standing gap in late-stage capital and exit pathways, it will only work if companies see Singapore as a viable place to raise capital at scale.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: If many of these companies are already anchored in Nasdaq or other exchanges, are we building liquidity here or just plugging into it?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: What are the opportunities Singapore can seize as companies, especially those exposed to geopolitical tensions and are looking for diversification, choose where they are listed?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This then leads to a broader question about market structure.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Today, we have the Catalist, the SGX Main Board, and now potentially the GLB.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: A strong capital market should not just have multiple boards, but a clear role for each.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Where does this leave the SGX Main Board in the overall structure?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Is there a meaningful difference between the GLB and the SGX Main Board?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Is the GLB meant to be an aspirational pathway for companies that grow through SGX or is it primarily a separate lane to attract already mature issuers from outside?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Because depending on the answer, it will shape how companies view SGX as a place to start and grow.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: More activity at the top end will naturally create spillover demand for banking, research, asset management and other services.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But based on the Bill, much of the immediate work will be in compliance, governance and advisory functions.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: If this Bill is to make a real difference, we also need to see deeper capabilities develop in research, investing and capital deployment.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It may also be useful to build capabilities here, for example, by allowing more use of forward-looking statements under safe harbour provisions and in how analysts and investors assess businesses that are still loss-making but growing.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Otherwise, we may end up servicing these listings, but not really building the depth of understanding needed to value them properly.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Importantly, where will these activities and jobs sit?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Will they be anchored here in Singapore or will the core activities still take place elsewhere?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I would also like to seek clarification on whether MAS has consulted companies on the regulatory landscape improvement and support network that the GLB prospects may have raised prior to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Companies do not just choose markets based on liquidity.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In markets like the US, investors are more familiar with R&D-heavy companies, deep tech firms and founder-led businesses with longer growth horizons.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: If we want to attract similar companies, it is not just about creating a new board, but whether companies and investors choose to be active here and whether our own market is ready.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Are we building enough investor depth, research coverage and understanding of these sectors?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, it is noted that MAS will retain much regulatory discretion in the administration of the GLB.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: We need to ensure that this flexibility and discretion do not come at the expense of clarity and investor confidence because Singapore has always competed on clarity, not ambiguity.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Otherwise, uncertainty over the applicable compliance framework may affect confidence, liquidity and valuation.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But success is not how many names we bring onto the board.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It is whether we bring real activity here – real trading, real capital and real investor participation.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Because in the end, markets are not defined by structure, but by where activity takes place.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: With these points, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Companies chose where to list and in doing so, they chose where value will be created, where liquidity would sit and where their story will be told.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, broad capital is global, deep liquidity is concentrated and the companies shaping the future, particularly in technology and innovation, are not bound by geography.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They go where capital is deepest, coverage is strongest and where they are understood.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This creates a structural challenge for Singapore, not because we lack strong institutions or capability or credibility, but because the gravitational pull of global capital, particularly for high-growth and technology companies, is traditionally not centred here due to investor culture, risks, platform dominance, regulatory infrastructure and talent, among other factors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The GLB offers a response to this reality.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not an attempt to out-compete the largest capital markets in the world.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a recognition that we must evolve our role within them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a more uncertain and fragmented global environment, it is imperative that Singapore continues to strengthen our position as a trusted and relevant financial hub.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Listings typically involve overlapping and sometimes disjointed disclosure standards, liability frameworks and regulatory timelines.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These can add significant coordination, complexity and cost.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I appreciate the intent of these amendments to better align processes and reduce duplication.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are practical steps that can reduce friction.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Southeast Asia continues to produce high-growth firms, particularly in tech, many seek listing opportunities in the US.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The GLB ensures that even as these companies pursue global capital, they can do so without losing access to regional investors, proximity to core markets and the strategic appeal that comes from being anchored in both Western and Asian ecosystems.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is also hoped that it will boost SGX's IPO pipeline and competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This ensures that our market is not merely a point of access but a point of participation where Singapore has a stake in the growth of these companies.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Rather than accessing such opportunities only through foreign markets, our capital can engage through our own infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By enabling companies to access US capital markets while maintaining a listing presence on SGX as well, we position Singapore not as an alternative but reinforce our role as a gateway economy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have long positioned ourselves as a hub for flows of capital, talent and ideas.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The GLB extends that logic into capital markets.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we must be clear-eyed about the risks and limitations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under the current structure, the listing on Nasdaq is an anchor.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The listing on SGX is not designed to stand independently.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If price discovery generally happens in the US due to deeper liquidity, what role can Singapore play beyond access?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If trading volumes concentrate in the US, how can we ensure our market also remains active rather than symbolic, given lower trading liquidity?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Otherwise, the requirement may become a hurdle that limits uptake and the default may be re-allocation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, preparing companies for the realities of the US market.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This means that the pool of companies which qualify for the GLB may not be large.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The question is also whether these companies are ready to go live as a public company in a US-led market environment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That means having the governance disclosure controls, investor relations capability and financial reporting discipline to withstand a cadence of scrutiny from sophisticated analysts, investor base regulators and the media.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Companies must also get used to new success metrics beyond revenue, especially tech firms.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If the GLB is to succeed, readiness cannot be treated as a compliance checklist, but instead be complemented with a capability building agenda.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The expectations of US markets may not always be aligned with the realities of companies emerging from Asia, many of which operate in different languages and times zones.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While operating in this environment will force companies to demonstrate a different level of robustness that is recognised more globally, whether by investors, partners or talent, I would like to ask how we are preparing our Singaporean companies for this transition beyond simply exposing them to the opportunity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And is there a supporting role that Singapore can play for Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) companies which intend to pursue a GLB listing?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Government should not be actively interfering or shaping a company's entry into capital markets, where possible, will we consider partnering with industry to develop structures to bridge capability gaps?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This leads to my third point: translating listings into tangible economic value for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It should be measured by the extent to which those listings translate into tangible economic value for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When a company lists, value is created across multiple areas, including capital formation, professional and support services, investor participation and longer-term ecosystem development.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened to see that there are mechanisms within the GLB that seek to anchor value locally.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It ensures that Singapore-based investors are not merely trading these securities but are participating in the formation of capital itself.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It creates allocation to local institutions and engagement with regional investor base.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The listing activities itself generates ecosystem value – from due diligence to legal structuring, underwriting and advisory, accounting and compliance, research and coverage.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These create new professional opportunities, build expertise and deepen Singapore's capabilities in handling cross-border listings.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A listing presence combined with investor engagement can, hopefully, encourage the development of regional headquarter functions and closer integration with Singapore's financial and business ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While not guaranteed, these are pathways through which listing activities can translate into longer-term economic contribution.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we must be realistic about the limits.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If analysts' coverage, investor engagement and prospectus requirements are primarily US-led, then much of the influence over valuation and requirements for US capabilities and professional services will sit outside of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do we have any plans to deepen local participation, both from investors and institutions attracting capital from other parts of Asia so that Singapore's role can grow?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For professional services, given familiarity with US laws and systems, would be necessary, how can we support local professionals to secure a share of the work generated?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And do we have any plans on an inter-agency effort that focuses on translating listing presence into broader corporate activity within Singapore?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the draft Bill and rules provide for regulatory cooperation and timely disclosure across both markets, there remains practical, operational questions of how this will work in moments of stress.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will cross-border investigation and enforcement operate in practice when the same event affects investors in both jurisdictions, depending on whether it is first detected in the US or in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
